chapter.title: Choosing who to watch and where to look

cards.body:
Your clipping service cannot read every paper in the city. You hand them a stack of 5 and say: only these, and only the pages where news actually appears. **Pick few rivals and the exact pages that change when something real happens.**

Picture the stack on the desk. The price list page and the *what's new* page are dog-eared. The glossy front cover is untouched. It looks the same every morning.
cards.simpler: Imagine you pay someone to read the newspapers for you and cut out the stories that matter. They cannot read every paper in town. So you hand them a stack of 5 and say: only these, and only the pages where real news shows up. **Pick few rivals and the exact pages that change when something real happens.** The price list page and the what's new page are worn from use. The shiny front cover looks the same every morning.

cards.prompt: You run a small bakery. You hire a clipper to watch your rival across the street, who has a website. Which page do you hand them?

options.text: The About Us page with the founder's story
The homepage with the big croissant photo

whyNot.a: That's the history, not the news: a founder's story was written once and will likely stay the same for years.
whyNot.c: That's the shop window, not the notice board: a homepage is built to look good, not to announce changes.

cards.reteach: A page is worth watching only if it changes when something real happens. Prices change when they change prices. A founder's story and a hero photo rarely move, so they tell you nothing new.

cards.title: Who, and which page
cards.body:
Start with 3 to 5 competitors. Not 10. The ones a customer would actually compare you against this month.

For each one, find 1 or 2 pages that **move when the business moves**. The pricing page changes when prices change. The *changelog*, a list of what's new in the product with the newest item at the top, changes when they ship. The careers page changes when they hire.

A blog can work too, but it is looser. A post about summer reading habits is not competitor news.
cards.simpler:
Start with 3 to 5 competitors, not 10. Choose the ones a customer would really compare you against this month.

For each one, find 1 or 2 pages that **move when the business moves**. The pricing page changes when prices change. The changelog, a list of what's new in the product with the newest item at the top, changes when they release something. The careers page changes when they hire.

A blog can work too, but it is looser. A post about summer reading is not competitor news.

cards.title: Tidewater on a Tuesday
cards.body:
Say you sell scheduling software and your closest rival is a company called Tidewater. You watch 2 pages: their pricing page and their changelog.

One Tuesday the changelog gains a line: "Two-way sync with Google Calendar." The same day the homepage photo changes from a woman at a laptop to a man at a laptop.

Only one of those is news. Your clipper should hand you the sync line, and never mention the laptop.
cards.simpler:
Say you sell scheduling software and your closest rival is a company called Tidewater. You watch 2 of their pages: the pricing page and the changelog.

One Tuesday a new line appears in the changelog: "Two-way sync with Google Calendar." The same day, the homepage photo changes from a woman at a laptop to a man at a laptop.

Only one of those is news. Your clipper should hand you the sync line and never mention the laptop photo.

cards.prompt: You have picked 4 competitors. Which watch list should you give the agent?

options.text: 4 competitors, 2 pages each: pricing and changelog, 8 pages total
4 competitors, every page you can find on each site, about 60 pages
4 competitors, the homepage of each, 4 pages total

whyNot.b: That's the whole newspaper, not the clippings: 60 pages means 60 chances for noise, and a summary nobody reads.
whyNot.c: That's the shop window again: homepages are designed to look good and rarely announce real changes.

cards.reteach: Few rivals, and for each the 1 or 2 pages that change when something real happens. Pricing and changelog are the safest bets. Everything else is extra noise for the agent to wade through.

cards.title: Why fewer beats more
cards.body:
Every page you add is a chance for a false alarm. Cookie banners get reworded. Testimonials rotate. A date stamp ticks over. 50 pages of that and the daily note becomes a wall you stop reading.

Be exact about the address too. The site is the newspaper. The page is where the story runs. Write the full address, the part after the slash included, like **/pricing** rather than the bare site name.

Next to each address, write one line on why it is worth reading. If you cannot write the line, drop the page.
cards.simpler:
Every page you add is one more chance for a false alarm. Cookie banners get reworded. Customer quotes rotate. A date ticks over. Watch 50 pages like that and the daily note becomes a wall you stop reading.

Be exact about the address too. The site is the newspaper. The page is where the story runs. Write the full address, including the part after the slash, like **/pricing** instead of just the site name.

Next to each address, write one line on why it matters. If you cannot write that line, drop the page.

cards.body: Mara adds a rival's homepage because "that's where they'd announce big things." Every single morning the agent reports a change. It is the customer quote carousel, picking a new quote on each load. After a week she stops opening the note. **A page that changes every day is noise, not news.** If a page fires daily, swap it for the pricing or changelog page.
cards.simpler: Mara adds a rival's homepage because "that's where they'd announce big things." Every morning the agent reports a change. It is the customer quote box, which shows a different quote each time the page loads. After a week she stops opening the note. **A page that changes every day is noise, not news.** If a page fires every day, swap it for the pricing or changelog page instead.

cards.prompt: For 10 days straight the agent reports a change on one competitor's page. What is the most likely story?

options.text: The competitor is shipping something new every day, so keep watching it closely
The page has rotating content, so swap it for a page that only changes on real events
You need more pages from that site to understand the pattern

whyNot.a: That's reading noise as news: real businesses rarely change prices or ship a feature 10 days in a row.
whyNot.c: That's more newspaper, not better clippings: adding pages multiplies the noise instead of removing it.

cards.reteach: A good page is quiet most days and loud when something real happens. If it is loud every day, something on it is rotating or auto-generated. Replace it, do not pile more pages on top.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Watch 3 to 5 rivals, and for each one pick 1 or 2 exact pages that **only change when the business does**: pricing, changelog, careers. Fewer good pages beat a list of 50, because every extra page is another chance for a false alarm.
cards.simpler: Watch 3 to 5 rivals. For each one, pick 1 or 2 exact pages that **only change when the business does**: pricing, changelog, careers. A few good pages beat a list of 50. Every extra page is one more chance for a false alarm, and enough false alarms make you stop reading the note at all.

cards.body: Open one competitor's site right now. Find their pricing or changelog page. Paste the exact address into a note, with one line on why it is worth reading. That is the first row of your watch list.
cards.simpler: Open one competitor's website right now. Find their pricing page or their changelog, the list of what's new in the product. Copy the exact address into a note. Next to it, write one line on why that page is worth reading. That is the first row of your watch list. The rest can wait until you have this one down.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now write a list of 3 to 5 competitors with 1 or 2 exact web addresses each, and say why each page is worth reading.
